content: 1. Training focused on gait, balance, coordination, or functional tasks is referred to as balance and functional exercises. These exercises aim to improve specific aspects of physical function, such as walking techniques, balance systems, and task-specific activities. 2. The risk of bias in studies was assessed using Cochrane’s Risk of Bias tool, as outlined in the Cochrane Handbook. This tool evaluates the methodological quality of studies to ensure reliable results. 3. Funnel plots were constructed and visually inspected to assess potential publication bias in the included studies. 4. The quality of evidence was evaluated using the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) approach. Evidence was categorized as high, moderate, low, or very low based on five factors: risk of bias, inconsistency of effect, indirectness, imprecision, and publication bias. 5. Summary of findings tables were prepared to present the results clearly. Standardized qualitative statements were used to describe the combinations of effect size and certainty of evidence. 6. For exercise interventions, the rate of falls was reduced by 23% (95% CI: 17% to 29%) in the general population. For every 1,000 people followed over one year, the number of falls was 655 (95% CI: 604 to 706) in the intervention group compared to 850 in the usual care group. 7. In populations with no specific selection criteria, the number of falls was 466 (95% CI: 430 to 503) per 1,000 people in the intervention group compared to 605 in the usual care group. 8. Exercise programs included in the analysis often focused on a single primary exercise category, such as gait, balance, and functional training, but could also include secondary exercise categories. 9. Gait training involves correcting walking techniques and practicing changes in pace, level, and direction. Balance training focuses on transferring body weight and challenging specific balance systems. Functional training emphasizes task-specific activities tailored to individual needs. 10. Resistance training involves muscle contractions against resistance (e.g., body weight or external weights) to improve muscular strength. These programs are assessment-based, tailored, and progressively advanced. 11. Tai Chi (3D training) incorporates upright posture, weight transfers, and controlled movements through three spatial planes. Dance-based 3D training emphasizes dynamic movement patterns and speeds in a fluid, repetitive manner. 12. General physical activity, such as walking, is defined as any movement produced by skeletal muscles that significantly increases energy expenditure. Recommendations on intensity, frequency, and duration are necessary to optimize performance. 13. The relationship between physical activity and frailty prevention was investigated in one RCT with a 12-month follow-up. Frailty was defined by the presence of three or more Fried criteria: unintentional weight loss, exhaustion, low physical activity, slow walking speed, and poor grip strength. 14. The association between physical activity and sarcopenia prevention was examined in one longitudinal study with a 48-month follow-up. Sarcopenia was defined as low muscle mass, low muscle strength, and/or low physical performance. 15. Four RCTs investigated the effects of physical activity on frailty-related outcomes, such as muscle mass, physical function, and muscle strength. Sixteen out of 18 comparisons showed positive effects, one showed neutral effects, and one showed negative effects. 16. Two RCTs examined the effects of physical activity on sarcopenia-related outcomes, including muscle strength and muscle mass. The evidence was graded as low due to imprecision and small sample sizes. 17. The classification of physical activity and exercise programs was based on the Prevention of Falls Network Europe (ProFANE) taxonomy. Categories included gait and balance training, resistance training, flexibility, 3D exercises (e.g., Tai Chi, dance), general physical activity, endurance, and other types of exercise. 18. The quality of evidence was assessed using the GRADE framework, considering factors such as risk of bias, inconsistency, imprecision, indirectness, and publication bias. Random-effects meta-analyses were conducted to summarize the effects of physical activity when multiple studies were available. 19. The search for systematic reviews on sarcopenia and frailty prevention included studies published between 2008 and 2019. Titles and abstracts were screened independently by two reviewers, and disagreements were resolved through discussion or consultation with a third reviewer. 20. Since no eligible systematic reviews were found, individual studies were included instead. Data extraction was performed by one reviewer and checked by a second reviewer. Outcomes relevant to sarcopenia and frailty were extracted and summarized. 21. The evidence suggests that physical activity may reduce the risk of falls and improve frailty-related outcomes, but the certainty of evidence varies depending on the study design, sample size, and methodological quality.
